summary: DHCPv4 Leasequery lets a requestor ask about existing address bindings, but only one binding at a time. This document extends it to transfer many bindings in bulk. The bulk transfer runs over TCP.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking one question at a time about who is using which address, you ask for the whole list in one go.

questions: how to query many dhcp leases at once
how does dhcp bulk leasequery use tcp
what port does bulk leasequery use
subtitle: Lets a relay agent or access concentrator pull many DHCPv4 lease bindings from a server over one TCP connection.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 Leasequery can only ask about one binding at a time, which does not scale when thousands of clients sit behind a relay agent that has lost its lease state.
tldr.mechanism: The requestor opens a TCP connection to the server on port 67 and sends a DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY. The server streams back one message per matching binding and ends with a DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE.
tldr.outcome: A requestor can rebuild its state before traffic arrives, and can limit the transfer by time window. It is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 7724.

facts.label: Framing prefix
facts.value: 2 octets, message size in network byte order

today: RFC 6926 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7724. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Bulk Leasequery
sections.content:
DHCPv4 servers hold the authoritative record of which client has which IPv4 address. Relay agents sit between clients and servers and often cache lease information they see, for example to prevent spoofing by DHCPv4 clients and to install routes. When a relay agent reboots, that cache is frequently lost.

The Leasequery protocol (RFC 4388) lets an outside entity ask a server about one address or client. Its queries are data driven: the relay agent asks when traffic arrives. That does not scale well with thousands of clients, or when the relay agent must rebuild its data before it processes traffic.

RFC 6926 adds queries that can each return many bindings, and moves them to TCP for efficient transfer of what may be many thousands of bindings. The design goals include getting information before data starts, reducing the need for caching and negative caching, keeping anti-spoofing in the fast path, and minimizing data sent. The last goal is met by query-start-time and query-end-time, so a device that saved its state periodically can recover just what changed since.
sections.eli5: When a helper forgets everything after a nap, it is faster to hand it the whole list than to let it ask about people one at a time.

sections.title: How a Bulk Query Works
sections.content:
A requestor opens a TCP connection to a DHCPv4 server on port 67 and sends a DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY message. It needs the server address by configuration or other means and unicast reachability. No relaying of Bulk Leasequery messages is specified.

The server finds the matching bindings and returns each as either DHCPLEASEACTIVE (the address is currently leased) or DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED (the server controls the address but no client has it now). When finished, it sends DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE. If the connection is lost midway, the query must be retried, because there is no way to learn how much the requestor already received.

A request has exactly one primary query: by MAC address, by Client-identifier, by Remote ID, by Relay-ID, or for all configured IP addresses (signalled by the absence of any other primary query). Any of them can be narrowed by a query start time, a query end time, and a VPN-ID, each at most once. Without a VPN-ID only the default (global) VPN is searched.

The TCP connection is only for the bulk query. It is not an alternative way for clients to get DHCPv4 service, and the existing UDP DHCPv4 transmission is left alone.
sections.eli5: You ask the server one big question, it sends back one answer card per match, and a final card that says 'that is all'.

sections.title: TCP Message Framing
sections.content:
TCP is a byte stream, so the receiver needs to know where each message ends. On a Bulk Leasequery connection, two octets holding the message size in network byte order are prepended to each DHCPv4 message. The size is a 16-bit unsigned integer, so the maximum message size is 65535 octets. After that prefix the message is a normal RFC 2131 DHCPv4 message, so existing code can handle the contents easily.

The framed format is not compatible with UDP. If a TCP-framed request were sent over UDP, its protocol fields would be offset by the size prefix and it may not be valid.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a sticker on the front saying how long it is, so the reader knows where one message stops and the next begins.

sections.title: New Message Types and Options
sections.content:
The dhcp-message-type option gets two new values, 14 for DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY and 15 for DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE. Seven new options carry the extra data:

  • status-code (151): a one-octet code and an optional UTF-8 message. Codes are Success 000, UnspecFail 001, QueryTerminated 002, MalformedQuery 003 and NotAllowed 004. Its scope is a single reply, or the whole request when it appears in DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE.
  • base-time (152): the server's current absolute time when it built the message. Other time values in the reply are relative to it.
  • start-time-of-state (153): seconds before the base-time at which the address entered its current state. It MUST NOT be an absolute time.
  • query-start-time (154) and query-end-time (155): absolute times, in the server's time context, that bound which changed bindings are returned.
  • dhcp-state (156): a finer-grained state than active or unassigned.
  • data-source (157): a flags octet whose REMOTE bit says whether the most recent change happened on the answering server (0, local) or another server (1, remote).

The VSS type table from RFC 6607 is extended with type 254, meaning all VPNs (wildcard). Types 2 to 253 stay unassigned and 255 remains the global, default VPN.
sections.eli5: The new options are extra labels on each answer: whether it worked, what time it is on the server, what state the address is in, and which server knows about it.

sections.title: What the Requestor Does
sections.content:
The requestor connects, and if that fails it MAY retry. Each DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY MUST have an xid unique on its connection, and every reply to it carries the same xid. The query SHOULD include a dhcp-parameter-request-list naming the options it wants, which SHOULD include base-time, dhcp-lease-time, start-time-of-state and client-last-transaction-time.

The requestor MUST be ready for many replies per query and MUST NOT assume any ordering. If a reply has an xid that matches no outstanding query, it MUST close the connection. The server includes the server-identifier option in the first reply only, and the requestor MUST cache it and apply it to later replies. A DHCPLEASEUNKNOWN message MUST NOT appear in a bulk response.

Because the server and requestor clocks may differ, the requestor has to keep two time contexts. The base-time is in the server's context and is a good value to save for a later query-start-time. If several servers answer about one address, a SHOULD-level algorithm picks the better record: prefer the later client-last-transaction-time, otherwise compare it with or use start-time-of-state, and if still tied prefer the record whose REMOTE flag is local.

One connection MAY carry several queries, each with a unique xid, and replies may be interleaved. A requestor that cannot handle interleaving MUST NOT send a second query before the first completes. When finished it SHOULD close the connection gracefully after the last DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE. If the connection or the data stream stalls, a timer of BULK_LQ_DATA_TIMEOUT starts and the requestor SHOULD terminate the connection when it expires.
sections.eli5: The asker numbers each question, keeps track of which answers belong to which question, and when two servers disagree it believes the one with the newer news.

sections.title: What the Server Does
sections.content:
Servers listen on TCP port 67 by default and MUST be able to limit the number of concurrent connections. The default BULK_LQ_MAX_CONNS is 10, and connections over that limit SHOULD be closed immediately. Servers MAY restrict which requestors, and which query types, are allowed, replying NotAllowed or just closing the connection.

Every request MUST end with a DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE where one can be sent. It MUST carry a status-code option if the end was not successful, and SHOULD NOT if it was. A query with no matches is still a success. The server MUST NOT send more than one message per IP address in a response, and the order is up to the server.

A request with a non-zero ciaddr, yiaddr or siaddr gets MalformedQuery. A request with more than one primary query gets NotAllowed. Active bindings answer the MAC address, Client-identifier, Remote ID and Relay-ID queries. For the all-addresses query every configured address is returned exactly once: DHCPLEASEACTIVE if bound, DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED if not.

The message type follows the dhcp-state value: ACTIVE gives DHCPLEASEACTIVE, anything else gives DHCPLEASEUNASSIGNED. A binding counts as changed in a time window if its client-last-transaction-time or start-time-of-state fell within it. For idle connections the server starts a BULK_LQ_DATA_TIMEOUT timer after the final reply and closes the connection when it expires. A server aborting a query SHOULD signal QueryTerminated.
sections.eli5: The server only lets approved askers in, answers each address once, and always says 'done' at the end. If an asker sits silent too long, it hangs up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Bulk Leasequery inherits the threats of DHCPv4 (RFC 2131) and the Leasequery recommendations of RFC 4388. TCP adds new risks: SYN flooding can use up a server's connections, and a malicious requestor can hold connections open with invalid, partial or no queries. The RFC recommends limiting connection sources, the number of connections and in-process queries, and how long an idle connection stays open.

Two issues get explicit mention. First, information must not reach unauthorized requestors, so servers SHOULD restrict connections and messages to certain requestors, and the typical DHCPv4 client SHOULD NOT be able to get a response. Some technique to prevent such access MUST exist wherever it is deployed. Second, data should not be disrupted in transit. Flows SHOULD cross only secured networks, and if they must cross unsecured ones they MUST use connections secured by means external to DHCP, such as VPNs.

DHCP authentication (RFC 3118) MUST NOT be used to secure these messages, because it was designed for UDP and would not protect the message framing.
sections.eli5: The seating chart is private, so only trusted helpers should get it, and it should travel through a locked tunnel rather than the open street.

items.label: DHCPBULKLEASEQUERY
items.desc: dhcp-message-type value for the bulk request.

items.label: DHCPLEASEQUERYDONE
items.desc: dhcp-message-type value that ends a query.

items.label: base-time
items.desc: Server's absolute time when the message was built.

items.label: start-time-of-state
items.desc: Seconds before base-time that the state began.

items.label: query-start-time
items.desc: Only bindings changed on or after this time.

items.label: query-end-time
items.desc: Only bindings changed on or before this time.

items.label: data-source
items.desc: Whether the latest change was local or remote.

items.label: AVAILABLE
items.desc: Address is available to the local DHCPv4 server.

items.label: ACTIVE
items.desc: Address is assigned to a DHCPv4 client.

items.label: RELEASED
items.desc: Lease was released by the DHCPv4 client.

items.label: ABANDONED
items.desc: Server or client flagged the address as unusable.

items.label: RESET
items.desc: Lease was freed by some external agent.

items.label: REMOTE
items.desc: Address is available to a remote DHCPv4 server.
